newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Data, comments dash German rate cut hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Data, comments dash German rate cut hopes.

text.p: Hopes for a near-term German interest rate cut were dashed on Friday when economic data revealed higher inflation and the Bundesbank's vice president stressed rates would be kept steady in the coming weeks.

Economists largely agreed the rare comment from vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, plus higher than predicted state cost of living statistics, strongly hinted the timing for an easing, which many still expect this year, had been extended.

"If inflation rates do not fall further, we will likely see a stagnation on interest rates," said Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt, adding that Bundesbank officials had recently signalled the group would prefer stable rates.
The year's first glimpse of inflation data coming from the states of Bavaria and Baden-Wuerttemberg showed annual increases of 1.6 and 1.7 percent, clearly disappointing markets.
Similarly German import prices, showing a 0.8 percent rise on the month and a two percent rise on the year in December, were also worrying, traders said.

Bundesbank vice president Gaddum, whose board position and reluctance to speak lend his comments particular weight, poured more cold water on revived rate cut talk when he explained the reasons for Friday's unusual money market liquidity injection.

An injection of 3.2 billion marks ($1.95 billion) in extra funds was to pull money market rates off highs of 3.20 percent. But the step also indicated that "German monetary policy would remain unchanged", Gaddum said.

Stefan Schneider, economist at Banque Paribas in Frankfurt said the inflation rates, fuelled largely by higher oil and gas prices "took away the capital markets' feeling everything is hunky dory with everyone thinking inflation is no problem".

But economists also warned against an overinterpretation of the data, saying administrative costs were often to blame for higher January inflation rates. "It does not signal an early resurgence of inflationary pressures," Merrill's Kraemer said.

Several British economists bet on a cut very soon, saying inflationary pressures were seen to be under control still and the Bundesbank had little choice but to cut rates again to help Germany's sluggish economy.
"An easing is inevitable" particuarly in light of expected record high jobless rates, said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB in London, arguing that action would dictated by events.

Economists also did not see eye to eye on Gaddum's comments. Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ in London, said Gaddum's words on Friday should not be overinterpreted. But Schneider disagreed, saying Gaddum was generally a very good guide on the policy making mood at the Bundesbank.

More importantly, German economists argued that the Bundesbank would be loathe to cut rates only to stimulate the economy, as the central bank's mandate was to ensure price stability, not pump up the economy.
"If they cut now in spite of the statements they would implicitly be accepting the argument that rate cuts do help the unemployment rate," Schneider said.
Others agreed that there was already quite enough liquidity in the economy and that a 10 basis point rate cut by the Bundesbank would not prompt businesses to hire new employees.

A Reuters poll earlier in the week showed a majority of economists saw an easing in this economic cycle. Some of them said a money market rate cut was still possible as the Bundesbank eyed both the mark's exchange rate and French interest rates carefully.
The German discount rate stands at 2.50 percent, the Lombard rate at 4.50 percent and the main money market rate, the repo, is at three percent.
